content.title: About
content.content: Raw macadamia nuts are the edible seeds of the macadamia tree (Macadamia integrifolia and Macadamia tetraphylla), native to Australia and cultivated extensively in Hawaii. They have a buttery, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp, creamy texture, and are rich in monounsaturated fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Macadamia belongs to the Proteaceae family, along with almonds, cashews, and hazelnuts.
Macadamia nuts are among the most expensive nuts in the world due to limited production.
They contain about 75 % fat, higher than most other nuts.
Commercial cultivation began in Hawaii in the early 20th century.
Raw macadamia nuts are sold without any heat treatment, preserving their natural flavor.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of the fat in macadamia nuts is oleic and palmitoleic acid, which support heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B1 (thiamine)
items.content: Thiamine helps with energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Macadamias provide tocopherols and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cholesterol balance
items.content: Regular consumption may help lower LDL (bad) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: They contain magnesium, iron, and calcium, important for bones and muscles.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions, potentially severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Macadamia nuts are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: They contain oxalates, which can be a concern for people prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw macadamia nuts can be eaten as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or processed into macadamia butter. They are also popular in desserts and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store nuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard nuts that develop a rancid smell.
